name: Jaw-chewing with Falim gum 8 hours

card.summary: Hard-gum chewing for hours to bulk the masseter; muscle growth is plausible, jaw pain is reported.
card.note: Users report jaw pain and clicking; overgrowth of the masseter is documented with constant gum chewing.

quick.overview:
People chew very hard Turkish gum such as Falim for many hours daily, aiming for a bigger, wider masseter and stronger-looking jaw.

The muscle can enlarge with constant gum chewing, but no trial has tested the practice for appearance. Users report both gains and pain.
quick.mechanism: Repetitive heavy chewing loads the masseter, which can hypertrophy with heavy use.
quick.risks: Reported effects include jaw pain, popping, ear-area pressure and excess masseter bulk. Temporomandibular literature lists gum chewing as a suggested but unproven contributor to jaw problems.

chain: Hours of resistance chewing load the masseter
Wider, more defined lower face and jaw angle
angle.text: Practitioners use hard gum as resistance training for the chewing muscles, expecting a wider, stronger-looking jaw. Muscle enlargement from constant gum chewing is documented in clinical descriptions, while the size of the cosmetic effect from hard-gum marathons has not been measured [1].

lead: Extended Falim chewing is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which people chew Falim, a hard Turkish gum, for hours a day, in some accounts up to eight, with the aim of building the masseter, the main jaw-closing muscle. Because the masseter sits at the angle of the lower face, practitioners expect a larger muscle to widen and square the jawline and make the lower face look stronger.

The masseter is known to enlarge with heavy use: clinical descriptions list habitual clenching, bruxism and constant gum chewing as causes of masseter hypertrophy, which is usually painless and bilateral, can change facial shape and is sometimes associated with temporomandibular joint problems [1][2]. Forum users describe both enlargement they welcome and jaw pain they attribute to long sessions [3][4].

The practice sits in the jaw-and-lower-face part of looksmaxxing, which Wikipedia describes as an online movement that grew from incel message boards in the 2010s and spread on TikTok in the 2020s, with a defined jawline among the features practitioners assess.[9] It is often discussed beside mewing, a tongue-posture practice that the American Association of Orthodontists and other experts say has no evidence of improving the jaw, whereas chewing aims at muscle rather than bone.[10]
No clinical trial of marathon hard-gum chewing for appearance has been published.

paras: Practitioners chew one or several pieces of hard gum at once, for sessions that users in threads describe as lasting many hours. Some say gum softens too fast and move to stiffer gums or mastic.[3][5]

sections.h: How it is meant to improve appearance
paras: The masseter is the thick muscle at the angle of the lower jaw, so a larger one adds width and fullness to the lower face when seen from the front. Practitioners treat gum like a weight for the jaw: resistance chewing, repeated for long periods, loads the muscle as lifting loads other muscles, and a bigger muscle is expected to give a squarer, more masculine jaw outline.[1][4] Users also say they expect more symmetry.[4]
Because it needs only gum and no procedure, it belongs to the non-surgical end of looksmaxxing, which Wikipedia contrasts with hardmaxxing procedures such as jaw surgery.[9]

Wikipedia describes the masseter as one of the four muscles of mastication, with a superficial head arising from the zygomatic arch, a deep head attaching to the upper mandibular ramus and a smaller coronoid head, supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve. Contracting both sides raises the mandible to close the jaw [1]. Hypertrophy is linked to teeth clenching or grinding and to constant gum chewing, is usually soft and painless, and can cause facial asymmetry if the two sides enlarge unequally. It can be mistaken for parotid disease or dental infection, and patients often seek care because of comments about their appearance [1].

There is no single documented origin. Chewing resin is ancient: Wikipedia reports a roughly 5,000-year-old piece of birch bark tar with tooth imprints from Kierikki in Finland, and that the ancient Greeks chewed mastic.[6] Mastic is the resin of Pistacia lentiscus from the Greek island of Chios, used in traditional medicine for roughly 2,500 years, which softens and turns white when chewed; the Wikipedia article on the resin describes chewing as one of its earliest uses.[7] Commercial gum developed in the nineteenth century, and Wikipedia notes that William Semple patented a gum in 1869 intended to clean teeth and exercise the jaw.[6]

In the looksmaxxing setting, hard Turkish gum and mastic became discussion topics on forums such as looksmax.org, where threads compare Falim with mastic and ask where jaw discomfort comes from.[3][5] Wikipedia's coverage of looksmaxxing and of mewing, the better-known jaw practice, does not mention gum chewing, so the practice is documented mainly in forum posts rather than in news or encyclopedic sources.[9][10]
Users say the practice widens the face, strengthens the jaw and improves symmetry.[4] Some report enlargement large enough that they sought masseter botulinum toxin injections afterward.[4]
Others report discomfort. One thread describes pressure near the ear, jaw popping when yawning and pain even when eating bread after chewing sessions.[3]

Descriptions in forum threads are informal. Users chew one or several pieces of hard gum at once, in sessions that users in threads describe as lasting many hours, and some switch from sweeter gums to harder or resin gums when softer ones lose firmness quickly.[3][5] One user reports turning to masseter botulinum toxin after enlargement.[4] No measurements of change from the practice have been published.

Reference sources describe masseter hypertrophy from constant gum chewing, usually painless and bilateral, and note it may be linked to temporomandibular joint problems.[1] Descriptions of temporomandibular disorders list excessive gum chewing among suggested parafunctional habits, but state that no specific evidence supports it and that the role of parafunction is debated.[2]

Wikipedia's article on temporomandibular joint dysfunction lists excessive gum chewing among parafunctional habits, along with bruxism, and states that the link between parafunction and the disorder is debated. It describes typical symptoms as dull, often one-sided jaw pain worse with chewing or yawning, clicking or popping (common also in people without pain), and limited opening, and says clinicians generally prefer reversible management and that evidence for treatments is weak [2].

Clinicians treating bruxism, the other common cause of masseter enlargement, describe masseter hypertrophy among its signs and compare muscle pain from clenching to pain after exercise, felt at the jaw angle or temple; Wikipedia says the link between bruxism and temporomandibular disorder is debated.[8] Botulinum toxin injected into the masseter is described as relaxing the muscle, with effects lasting about three months, and reduced power to chew solid food is a listed side effect when the masseter is injected.[8][11]

Users report pressure near the ear, popping of the jaw when yawning and pain when eating after long sessions.[3] Overgrowth of the masseter can change facial shape and cause asymmetry if the sides enlarge unequally, and one poster describes needing masseter botulinum toxin because the jaw became too big.[1][4] Temporomandibular literature lists gum chewing among suggested parafunctional habits, with the role of such habits described as debated.[2] The mastic article advises against mastic powder remedies for children, pregnant women and nursing mothers.[7]

Falim appears in threads that mix enthusiasm with troubleshooting: users posting that their faces look wider, others asking about ear pain, and comparison threads on whether mastic or Falim is better.[3][4][5] The practice is usually described by its own supporters as an inexpensive, non-surgical method, and is discussed alongside mewing and other jaw practices.[9][10]

Chewing resin has a long history. Wikipedia reports a roughly 5,000-year-old piece of birch bark tar with tooth imprints from Kierikki in Finland, and says the ancient Greeks chewed mastic, a resin from the mastic tree, which like birch tar is believed to have antiseptic properties [6]. Commercial gum developed mainly in the United States in the nineteenth century, and Wikipedia notes that William Semple patented a gum in 1869 intended to clean teeth and exercise the jaw [6]. Mastic gum is the gum that users compare with Falim in forum threads [5][6]. Wikipedia's chewing gum article does not discuss jaw muscle growth [6].

No studies found. Related background: clinical descriptions of masseter hypertrophy report that constant gum chewing can enlarge the muscle [1]. A small 2009 study cited on Wikipedia had 35 adult orthodontic patients chew gum for 10 to 15 minutes after meals for four weeks and reported that half reported no discomfort; it concerned bite contact, not appearance [6].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, Falim threads mix reports of visible jaw growth with reports of jaw pain.[3][4]

claims.claim: Hours of Falim chewing widens and strengthens the jaw
claims.believers: Users post that their faces are getting wider and stronger and that symmetry is improving.[4]
claims.experts: Clinical descriptions confirm the masseter can enlarge with constant gum chewing; no study has measured bony change or appearance outcomes from hard-gum marathons.[1]

claims.claim: Long chewing sessions can hurt the jaw joint
claims.believers: Users describe ear-area pressure, jaw popping and pain when eating after chewing.[3]
claims.experts: Temporomandibular literature lists gum chewing among suggested parafunctional habits, though evidence is described as lacking and the link debated.[2]

claims.believers: One user says masseter botulinum toxin was needed because the jaw became too big.[4]
claims.experts: Masseter hypertrophy is described as potentially changing facial shape and asymmetry.[1]

claims.claim: Mastic is a better gum than Falim for jaw training
claims.believers: Forum threads compare the two gums and ask which is better for hardness and durability.[5]
claims.experts: Mastic is a traditional Chios resin with a long history as chewing gum and an EMA-approved herbal use for indigestion; no study compares gums for masseter growth.[7]
